claim: In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), large motoneurons that innervate fast-contracting muscle fibers (F-type motoneurons) are vulnerable and degenerate in adulthood.
source: In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) the large motoneurons that innervate the fast-contracting muscle fibers (F-type motoneurons) are vulnerable and degenerate in adulthood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information about ALS pathology.

claim: Small motoneurons that innervate slow-contracting fibers (S-type motoneurons) are resistant and do not degenerate in ALS.
source: In contrast, the small motoneurons that innervate the slow-contracting fibers (S-type motoneurons) are resistant and do not degenerate.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information about ALS pathology, contrasting with F-type motoneurons.

claim: Intrinsic hyperexcitability of F-type motoneurons during early postnatal development has long been hypothesized to contribute to neural degeneration in the adult.
source: Intrinsic hyperexcitability of F-type motoneurons during early postnatal development has long been hypothesized to contribute to neural degeneration in the adult.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis that has been proposed in the field, representing existing scientific thinking.

claim: Excitability of F-type motoneurons was unchanged in neonatal mSOD1 mice.
source: Contrary to the standard hypothesis, excitability of F-type motoneurons was unchanged in the mutant mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's electrophysiological recordings in identified motoneuron subtypes.

claim: S-type motoneurons of mSOD1 mice display intrinsic hyperexcitability with lower rheobase and hyperpolarized spiking threshold.
source: Surprisingly, the S-type motoneurons of mSDO1 mice did display intrinsic hyperexcitability (lower rheobase, hyperpolarized spiking threshold).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's electrophysiological measurements.

claim: Early intrinsic hyperexcitability does not contribute to motoneuron degeneration in ALS.
source: As S-type motoneurons are resistant in ALS, we conclude that early intrinsic hyperexcitability does not contribute to motoneuron degeneration.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the observation that hyperexcitable S-type motoneurons are resistant while non-hyperexcitable F-type motoneurons are vulnerable.

claim: Glutamate excitotoxicity has long been suggested to contribute to the degeneration of motoneurons in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
source: Glutamate excitotoxicity has long been suggested to contribute to the degeneration of motoneurons in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
evidence: This is stated as established background knowledge in the field.

claim: Intrinsic hyperexcitability of motoneurons increases discharge probability and thereby calcium inflow.
source: Intrinsic hyperexcitability of motoneurons, which increases discharge probability and thereby calcium inflow, has been assumed to participate in the excitotoxic process (Ilieva et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a mechanism that has been proposed in the literature, supported by citation.

claim: It was recently suggested that hyperexcitability improves motoneuron survival.
source: However, it was recently suggested that hyperexcitability improves motoneuron survival (Saxena et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a recent alternative hypothesis from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Changes in excitability occur very early in mSOD1 mice.
source: Indeed, changes in excitability occur very early in mSOD1 mice (Elbasiouny et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citation.

claim: Motoneurons from mSOD1 embryos recorded in culture are hyperexcitable, recruited at lower current and display higher F–I gain.
source: Motoneurons from mSOD1 embryos recorded in culture are hyperexcitable (Pieri et al., 2003; Kuo et al., 2005): they are recruited at lower current and display higher F–I gain.
evidence: This is stated as previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: Martin et al. (2013) found that motoneurons in an in vitro preparation of mSOD1 embryonic cord are hyperexcitable due to reduced dendritic tree causing increased input resistance.
source: Similarly, Martin et al. (2013) found, in an in vitro preparation of mSOD1 embryonic cord, that motoneurons are also hyperexcitable: their dendritic tree is reduced causing an increase in input resistance.
evidence: This is stated as previous research findings, supported by citation.

claim: Hypoglossal motoneurons were reported to be hyperexcitable with increased F–I gain.
source: Hypoglossal motoneurons were reported to be hyperexcitable (F–I gain is increased, van Zundert et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as previous research findings, supported by citation.

claim: Pambo–Pambo et al. (2009) did not observe any change in spinal motoneuron input resistance, rheobase, or stationary gain, suggesting excitability was unchanged.
source: However, Pambo–Pambo et al. (2009) did not observe any change in spinal motoneuron input resistance, rheobase, or stationary gain suggesting that their excitability was unchanged.
evidence: This is stated as previous research findings, supported by citation.

claim: Quinlan et al. (2011) found that excitability of spinal motoneurons is homeostatically maintained despite an increase in input conductance.
source: In the same line, Quinlan et al. (2011) found that the excitability of spinal motoneurons is homeostatically maintained despite an increase in their input conductance (recruitment current and F–I gain unchanged).
evidence: This is stated as previous research findings, supported by citation.

claim: Bories et al. (2007) reported a decrease in input resistance causing spinal motoneurons to be hypoexcitable.
source: In contrast, Bories et al. (2007) reported a decrease in input resistance causing the spinal motoneurons to be hypoexcitable.
evidence: This is stated as previous research findings, supported by citation.

claim: The motor unit population is heterogeneous, even in neonates.
source: Until now, however, the fact that the motor unit population is heterogeneous, even in neonates (Jansen and Flatby, 1990), has never been taken into account.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citation.

claim: Motoneurons display different patterns of discharge during the second post-natal week both in rats and in mice.
source: Motoneurons innervate different types of muscle fibers and display different patterns of discharge during the second post-natal week both in rats (Russier et al., 2003) and in mice (Pambo–Pambo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citations.

claim: For liminal current pulses, discharge starts at pulse onset in some motoneurons (immediate firing pattern) but is delayed in others (delayed firing pattern).
source: Indeed, for liminal current pulses, the discharge starts at the pulse onset in some motoneurons (immediate firing pattern) but is delayed in others (delayed firing pattern).
evidence: This is stated as an observation about motoneuron behavior.

claim: Immediate firing spinal motoneurons innervate slow-contracting fibers (S-type motoneurons).
source: Here, we provide electrical, morphological and molecular evidence that immediate firing spinal motoneurons innervate slow-contracting fibers (S-type motoneurons) whereas delayed firing motoneurons innervate fast-contracting fibers (F-type motoneurons).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on multiple types of evidence.

claim: Delayed firing motoneurons innervate fast-contracting fibers (F-type motoneurons).
source: Here, we provide electrical, morphological and molecular evidence that immediate firing spinal motoneurons innervate slow-contracting fibers (S-type motoneurons) whereas delayed firing motoneurons innervate fast-contracting fibers (F-type motoneurons).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on multiple types of evidence.

claim: Only immediate firing motoneurons are hyperexcitable in neonatal mSOD1 mice.
source: We then investigated whether these two populations are equally affected in neonatal mSOD1 mice. We show that this is not the case: only the immediate firing motoneurons are hyperexcitable.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The rheobase of immediate firing motoneurons is decreased in mSOD1 mice because of a more hyperpolarized voltage threshold for spiking.
source: Their rheobase is decreased because of a more hyperpolarized voltage threshold for spiking.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The excitability of delayed firing motoneurons is unchanged in mSOD1 mice.
source: In sharp contrast, the excitability of the delayed firing motoneurons is unchanged.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's electrophysiological recordings.

claim: F-type motoneurons are vulnerable in ALS whereas S-type motoneurons are resistant.
source: Since the F-type motoneurons are vulnerable in ALS whereas the S-type motoneurons are resistant (Pun et al., 2006; Hegedus et al., 2008), the remarkably selective intrinsic hyperexcitality of S-type motoneurons in neonates indicates that intrinsic hyperexcitability is not an early event that triggers degeneration of the motoneurons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citations.

claim: Intrinsic hyperexcitability is not an early event that triggers degeneration of motoneurons.
source: Since the F-type motoneurons are vulnerable in ALS whereas the S-type motoneurons are resistant (Pun et al., 2006; Hegedus et al., 2008), the remarkably selective intrinsic hyperexcitality of S-type motoneurons in neonates indicates that intrinsic hyperexcitability is not an early event that triggers degeneration of the motoneurons.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: 63 out of 94 WT motoneurons (67%) exhibited the delayed firing pattern.
source: 63 out of 94 WT motoneurons (67%) exhibited this delayed firing pattern.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's recordings.

claim: 31 out of 94 WT motoneurons (33%) displayed the immediate firing pattern.
source: 31 out of the 94 WT motoneurons (i.e., 33%) displayed the immediate firing pattern.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's recordings.

claim: The input conductance is smaller in immediate firing motoneurons than in delayed firing ones.
source: On average, the input conductance is smaller, the rheobase is lower and the voltage threshold for spiking is more hyperpolarized in immediate firing motoneurons than in delayed firing ones and this occurs despite of the fact that the resting membrane potential is similar (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological measurements, as shown in Table 1.

claim: The rheobase is lower in immediate firing motoneurons than in delayed firing ones.
source: On average, the input conductance is smaller, the rheobase is lower and the voltage threshold for spiking is more hyperpolarized in immediate firing motoneurons than in delayed firing ones and this occurs despite of the fact that the resting membrane potential is similar (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological measurements, as shown in Table 1.

claim: The voltage threshold for spiking is more hyperpolarized in immediate firing motoneurons than in delayed firing ones.
source: On average, the input conductance is smaller, the rheobase is lower and the voltage threshold for spiking is more hyperpolarized in immediate firing motoneurons than in delayed firing ones and this occurs despite of the fact that the resting membrane potential is similar (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological measurements, as shown in Table 1.

claim: The resting membrane potential is similar between immediate and delayed firing motoneurons.
source: On average, the input conductance is smaller, the rheobase is lower and the voltage threshold for spiking is more hyperpolarized in immediate firing motoneurons than in delayed firing ones and this occurs despite of the fact that the resting membrane potential is similar (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological measurements, as shown in Table 1.

claim: Immediate firing motoneurons have wider action potentials than delayed firing motoneurons.
source: Moreover, immediate and delayed firing motoneurons display differences in the shape of their action potentials. Immediate firing motoneurons have wider action potentials and a longer relaxation time constant of their after-hyperpolarization (AHP) compared to delayed firing motoneurons (see Figure 1B and Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological measurements, shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: Immediate firing motoneurons have a longer relaxation time constant of their after-hyperpolarization (AHP) compared to delayed firing motoneurons.
source: Moreover, immediate and delayed firing motoneurons display differences in the shape of their action potentials. Immediate firing motoneurons have wider action potentials and a longer relaxation time constant of their after-hyperpolarization (AHP) compared to delayed firing motoneurons (see Figure 1B and Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological measurements, shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: The number of primary dendrites per motoneuron is similar in immediate and delayed firing motoneurons.
source: In these conditions, the number of primary dendrites (and thereby dendritic trees) per motoneuron is similar in immediate and delayed firing motoneurons (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's morphological analysis, as shown in Table 2.

claim: Delayed firing motoneurons have on average more branching points (44 ± 14, 26 to 72, N = 14) compared to immediate firing motoneurons (27 ± 13, 13 to 52, N = 10, p = 0.007).
source: In WT mice, delayed firing motoneurons have on average more branching points (44 ± 14, 26 to 72, N = 14) compared to the immediate firing motoneurons (27 ± 13, 13 to 52, N = 10, p = 0.007), larger total dendritic length and longer dendritic paths than immediate firing motoneurons (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's morphological analysis with statistical significance.

claim: Delayed firing motoneurons have larger total dendritic length than immediate firing motoneurons.
source: In WT mice, delayed firing motoneurons have on average more branching points (44 ± 14, 26 to 72, N = 14) compared to the immediate firing motoneurons (27 ± 13, 13 to 52, N = 10, p = 0.007), larger total dendritic length and longer dendritic paths than immediate firing motoneurons (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's morphological analysis, as shown in Table 2.

claim: Delayed firing motoneurons have longer dendritic paths than immediate firing motoneurons.
source: In WT mice, delayed firing motoneurons have on average more branching points (44 ± 14, 26 to 72, N = 14) compared to the immediate firing motoneurons (27 ± 13, 13 to 52, N = 10, p = 0.007), larger total dendritic length and longer dendritic paths than immediate firing motoneurons (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's morphological analysis, as shown in Table 2.

claim: Both immediate and delayed firing motoneurons are alpha-motoneurons and not gamma-motoneurons.
source: A body of evidence indicates that both immediate and delayed firing motoneurons are alpha-motoneurons (i.e., motoneurons that innervate extrafusal muscle fibers) and not gamma-motoneurons (i.e., motoneurons that innervate intrafusal muscle fibers).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence presented in the study.

claim: The soma sizes of both immediate and delayed firing motoneurons are in the range of alpha motoneurons.
source: First, the soma sizes (Table 2) of both immediate and delayed firing motoneurons are in the range of alpha motoneurons (see supplemental data in Friese et al. (2009) for the soma size distribution of alpha and gamma-motoneurons in P14 mice).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's morphological measurements compared to literature values.

claim: Immediate firing motoneurons have smaller soma areas than delayed firing motoneurons on average.
source: Note, however, that on average, immediate firing motoneurons have smaller soma areas than delayed firing motoneurons (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's morphological measurements, as shown in Table 2.

claim: Alpha-motoneurons, but not gamma-motoneurons, receive monosynaptic Ia inputs.
source: Second, since alpha-motoneurons, but not gamma-motoneurons, receive monosynaptic Ia inputs (Eccles et al., 1960), we checked whether immediate and delayed firing motoneurons receive such proprioceptive inputs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citation.

claim: VGlut1 is expressed in terminals from primary afferents but not in terminals from excitatory interneurons or descending fibers.
source: Subsequently, we stained the vesicular glutamate transporter 1 (VGlut1) since VGlut1 is expressed in terminals from primary afferents but not in terminals from excitatory interneurons or descending fibers (Oliveira et al., 2003; Friese et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citations.

claim: Both delayed and immediate firing motoneurons received proprioceptive terminals on the soma and proximal dendrites.
source: We observed that both delayed and immediate firing motoneurons received proprioceptive terminals on the soma and proximal dendrites (Figure 2A, arrows in insets).
evidence: This is a result from the study's immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NeuN is a known marker for alpha-motoneurons.
source: Third, we checked for the expression of the neuronal nuclear antigen (NeuN), a known marker for alpha-motoneurons (Friese et al., 2009; Shneider et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citations.

claim: Both immediate and delayed firing motoneurons expressed NeuN.
source: Both immediate and delayed firing motoneurons expressed NeuN (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the study's immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Estrogen-related receptor β (Errβ) is expressed in S-type but not in F-type motoneurons.
source: It has been suggested that the estrogen-related receptor β (Errβ) is expressed in S-type but not in F-type motoneurons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research.

claim: Chondrolectin (Chodl) is expressed in a fraction of F-type motoneurons but not in S-type motoneurons.
source: Conversely, chondrolectin (Chodl) is expressed in a fraction of F-type motoneurons but not in S-type motoneurons (Enjin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citation.

claim: All 6 investigated immediate firing motoneurons were Errβ-positive whereas all 8 delayed firing motoneurons were Errβ-negative.
source: Remarkably, all 6 investigated immediate firing motoneurons proved to be Errβ-positive whereas all 8 delayed firing motoneurons were Errβ-negative.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's immunohistochemical analysis.

claim: None of the 9 investigated immediate firing motoneurons expressed Chodl mRNA.
source: None of the 9 investigated immediate firing motoneurons did.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's in situ hybridization analysis.

claim: 7 out of 15 investigated delayed firing motoneurons were Chodl-positive whereas 8 were Chodl-negative.
source: 7 out of the 15 investigated delayed firing motoneurons were Chodl-positive whereas the remaining 8 were Chodl-negative.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's in situ hybridization analysis.

claim: The immediate firing motoneurons were all Errβ-positive and Chodl-negative as expected for S-type motoneurons.
source: Altogether, the immediate firing motoneurons were all Errβ-positive and Chodl-negative as expected for S-type.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the molecular marker analysis.

claim: The delayed firing motoneurons were all Errβ-negative and about half were Chodl-positive as expected for F-type motoneurons.
source: On the other hand, the delayed firing motoneurons were all Errβ-negative and about half of them were Chodl-positive whereas the other half were chondrolectine-negative as expected for F-type motoneurons (Enjin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the molecular marker analysis, supported by citation.

claim: The Chodl-positive motoneurons tended to display the highest rheobases.
source: Interestingly, the Chodl-positive motoneurons tended to display the highest rheobases (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from the study's combined electrophysiological and molecular analysis, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP9) is strongly expressed in motoneurons that are the most vulnerable to ALS.
source: Kaplan et al. (2014) recently showed that the matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP9) is strongly expressed in motoneurons that are the most vulnerable to ALS, that is, those of the large, fast contracting and fatigable (FF) motor units.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from recent research, supported by citation.

claim: The most resistant motoneurons (those that innervate slow contracting fibers) are devoid of MMP9.
source: Conversely, the most resistant motoneurons, that is, those that innervate the slow contracting fibers, were devoid of MMP9.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from recent research.

claim: All 5 investigated immediate firing motoneurons were MMP9 negative.
source: All 5 investigated immediate firing motoneurons were MMP9 negative (Figure 5A, first row).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 5 out of 10 investigated delayed firing motoneurons displayed strong MMP9 labelling.
source: In contrast, 5 out of the 10 investigated delayed firing motoneurons displayed a strong MMP9 labelling (Figure 5A, second row).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's immunohistochemical analysis, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The delayed firing motoneurons that express MMP9 tend to exhibit the largest input conductances and rheobases.
source: The delayed firing motoneurons that express MMP9 tend to exhibit the largest input conductances and rheobases (Figure 5B) suggesting that they innervate the largest motor units.
evidence: This is an observation from the study's combined electrophysiological and molecular analysis, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The immediate firing motoneurons are resistant during ALS.
source: These results indicate that the immediate firing motoneurons are resistant during ALS, in keeping with our identification as S-type motoneurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MMP9 expression pattern.

claim: 31 out of 49 mSOD1 motoneurons (63%) exhibited the delayed firing pattern.
source: 31 out of 49 mSOD1 motoneurons (63%) exhibited the delayed firing pattern (Figure 6A1) whereas the 18 remaining motoneurons (37%) displayed the immediate firing pattern (Figure 6A2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's recordings in mSOD1 mice.

claim: 18 out of 49 mSOD1 motoneurons (37%) displayed the immediate firing pattern.
source: 31 out of 49 mSOD1 motoneurons (63%) exhibited the delayed firing pattern (Figure 6A1) whereas the 18 remaining motoneurons (37%) displayed the immediate firing pattern (Figure 6A2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's recordings in mSOD1 mice.

claim: The proportion of delayed and immediate firing motoneurons is not different between WT and mSOD1 mice.
source: The proportion of delayed and immediate firing motoneurons is not different between WT and mSOD1 mice (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.5).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's analysis.

claim: The resting membrane potential, input conductance, action potential width and AHP relaxation time constant of each motoneuron subtype are unchanged in mSOD1 mice compared to WT mice.
source: Moreover, the resting membrane potential, the input conductance, the action potential width and the AHP relaxation time constant of each motoneuron subtype are unchanged in mSOD1 mice compared to WT mice (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological measurements, as shown in Table 1.

claim: The excitability of immediate firing motoneurons, but not delayed firing ones, is altered in mSOD1 mice.
source: Despite the unchanged input conductance, the excitability of the immediate firing motoneurons, but not of the delayed firing ones, is altered in mSOD1 mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's electrophysiological analysis.

claim: The slope of the linear regression of rheobase vs input conductance is significantly smaller in mSOD1 immediate firing motoneurons than in WT (15 vs 22 mV, t test p = 0.04, Chow test p = 0.0004).
source: However, in immediate firing motoneurons, the slope of the linear regressions is significantly smaller in mSOD1 mice than in WT mice (Figure 6B2, 15 vs 22 mV t test p = 0.04, Chow test p = 0.0004).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's statistical analysis, shown in Figure 6B2.

claim: The rheobase of immediate firing motoneurons is two times smaller in mSOD1 mice compared to WT mice on average.
source: On average the rheobase of immediate firing motoneurons is two times smaller in mSOD1 mice compared to WT mice (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological measurements, as shown in Table 1.

claim: The rheobase of delayed firing motoneurons is not significantly affected in mSOD1 mice.
source: On the other hand, the rheobase of delayed firing motoneurons is not significantly affected in mSOD1 mice (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological measurements, as shown in Table 1.

claim: The resting membrane potential of immediate firing motoneurons is unchanged in mSOD1 mice.
source: However, the resting membrane potential of immediate firing motoneurons is unchanged in mSOD1 mice (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological measurements, as shown in Table 1.

claim: The decrease in rheobase in mSOD1 immediate firing motoneurons is due to a hyperpolarization of the voltage threshold for spiking.
source: The decrease in rheobase in mSOD1 immediate firing motoneurons is instead due to an hyperpolarization of the voltage threshold for spiking (Table 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's electrophysiological measurements, as shown in Table 1.

claim: The difference between the voltage threshold for spiking and the resting membrane potential is smaller for immediate firing motoneurons in mSOD1 mice.
source: Accordingly, the difference between the voltage threshold for spiking and the resting membrane potential is smaller for the immediate firing motoneurons in mSOD1 mice (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological measurements, as shown in Table 1.

claim: The recruitment current on slow ramps was significantly smaller in mSOD1 mice only in immediate firing motoneurons.
source: The recruitment current on the slow ramps was very close to the rheobase measured using the current pulses (Table 1), and again, it was significantly smaller in mSOD1 mice only in the immediate firing motoneurons.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological measurements, as shown in Table 1.

claim: Mixed mode oscillations (MMOs) are related to the excitability state of motoneurons.
source: We have previously shown that mixed mode oscillations (MMOs) are related to the excitability state of motoneurons (Iglesias et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the authors' previous research, supported by citation.

claim: MMOs are caused by a relative deficit of sodium current with respect to potassium current, which is due to a slow sodium inactivation.
source: We have shown in a previous study (Iglesias et al., 2011) that MMOs are caused by a relative deficit of sodium current with respect to potassium current, which is due to a slow sodium inactivation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the authors' previous research, supported by citation.

claim: MMOs reflect a low excitability state.
source: MMOs therefore reflect a low excitability state.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from previous research.

claim: MMOs were observed in 49 out of 50 delayed firing motoneurons recorded in WT animals.
source: In the case of the delayed firing motoneurons, MMOs were observed nearly in all cells (49 out of 50) recorded in WT animals (Figure 7A1) and in all 31 mSOD1 motoneurons (Figure 7A2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological recordings.

claim: MMOs were observed in all 31 mSOD1 delayed firing motoneurons.
source: In the case of the delayed firing motoneurons, MMOs were observed nearly in all cells (49 out of 50) recorded in WT animals (Figure 7A1) and in all 31 mSOD1 motoneurons (Figure 7A2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological recordings.

claim: MMOs are encountered in nearly all WT immediate firing motoneurons (13 out of 15).
source: In the case of the immediate firing motoneurons, MMOs are encountered in nearly all WT motoneurons (13 out of 15, Figure 7B1) but they are absent in most mSOD1 motoneurons (MMOs are lacking in 8 out of 11 mSOD1 immediate firing motoneurons, Figure 7B2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological recordings.

claim: MMOs are absent in most mSOD1 immediate firing motoneurons (lacking in 8 out of 11).
source: In the case of the immediate firing motoneurons, MMOs are encountered in nearly all WT motoneurons (13 out of 15, Figure 7B1) but they are absent in most mSOD1 motoneurons (MMOs are lacking in 8 out of 11 mSOD1 immediate firing motoneurons, Figure 7B2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The proportion of immediate firing motoneurons exhibiting MMOs in mSOD1 is significantly reduced compared to WT motoneurons (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.003).
source: The proportion of immediate firing motoneurons exhibiting MMOs in mSOD1 is thus significantly reduced compared to WT motoneurons (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.003).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's analysis.

claim: The absence of MMOs in immediate firing motoneurons of mSOD1 mice indicates that these motoneurons are more excitable than in WT mice.
source: The absence of MMOs in the immediate firing motoneurons of mSOD1 mice further indicates that these motoneurons are more excitable than in WT mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MMO observations.

claim: The gain in the primary range of immediate firing motoneurons was not significantly different between WT (35 ± 22 Hz nA−1, N = 12) and mSOD1 mice (26 ± 8 Hz nA−1, N = 9, p = 0.7).
source: When a primary range could be observed in immediate firing motoneurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C2,D2, dark points), its slope was not significantly different between WT and mSOD1 mice (35 ± 22 Hz nA−1, 11–80 Hz nA−1, N = 12 for WT vs 26 ± 8 Hz nA−1, 16–41 Hz nA−1 for mSOD1, N = 9, p = 0.7).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological analysis.

claim: The gain in the primary range is largely determined by the AHP conductance.
source: Since the gain in the primary range is largely determined by the AHP conductance (Brownstone et al., 1992; Kernell, 2006; Manuel et al., 2006), this result suggests that the AHP conductance is unchanged in mSOD1 mice.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citations.

claim: The AHP conductance is unchanged in mSOD1 mice.
source: Since the gain in the primary range is largely determined by the AHP conductance (Brownstone et al., 1992; Kernell, 2006; Manuel et al., 2006), this result suggests that the AHP conductance is unchanged in mSOD1 mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gain measurements.

claim: The firing frequency reached 0.5 s after recruitment in delayed firing motoneurons is not different between WT (30 ± 7 Hz, N = 42) and mSOD1 mice (29 ± 6 Hz, N = 26).
source: However, we measured the firing frequency reached 0.5 s after the recruitment and we found that it is not different between delayed firing motoneurons of WT (30 ± 7 Hz, 17 to 49 Hz, N = 42) and mSOD1 mice (29 ± 6 Hz, 13 to 42 Hz, N = 26).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's electrophysiological analysis.

claim: In mSOD1 mice, delayed firing motoneurons are larger than immediate firing ones, similarly to WT mice.
source: In mSOD1 mice, similarly to WT mice, delayed firing motoneurons are larger than immediate firing ones (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is an observation from the study's morphological analysis, shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The morphology of the dendritic tree is affected specifically in immediate firing motoneurons in mSOD1 mice.
source: However the morphology of the dendritic tree is affected specifically in immediate firing motoneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's morphological analysis.

claim: The total dendritic length, length of dendritic paths and length of terminal segments are not different in delayed firing motoneurons of mSOD1 and WT mice (excluding one outlier).
source: If we exclude this outlayer motoneuron, the total dendritic length, the length of dendritic paths (Figure 8C1) and the length of terminal segments are not different in delayed firing motoneurons of mSOD1 and WT mice (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's morphological analysis, as shown in Table 2 and Figure 8C1.

claim: The total dendritic length of immediate firing motoneurons is 32% smaller in mSOD1 motoneurons than in WT motoneurons.
source: Their total dendritic length is 32% smaller in mSOD1 motoneurons than in WT motoneurons (Table 2) while the number of branching points is not significatively different (mSOD1 mice: 27 ± 14, 9–45, N = 5; WT mice: 27 ± 13, 13–52, N = 10, p = 0.8).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's morphological analysis, as shown in Table 2.

claim: The number of branching points in immediate firing motoneurons is not significantly different between mSOD1 (27 ± 14, N = 5) and WT mice (27 ± 13, N = 10, p = 0.8).
source: Their total dendritic length is 32% smaller in mSOD1 motoneurons than in WT motoneurons (Table 2) while the number of branching points is not significatively different (mSOD1 mice: 27 ± 14, 9–45, N = 5; WT mice: 27 ± 13, 13–52, N = 10, p = 0.8).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's morphological analysis.

claim: The dendritic paths of immediate firing motoneurons are on average 28% shorter in mSOD1 mice.
source: Consistently, the dendritic paths and terminal segments are on average 28% and 25% shorter, respectively, in mSOD1 mice (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's morphological analysis, as shown in Table 2.

claim: The terminal segments of immediate firing motoneurons are on average 25% shorter in mSOD1 mice.
source: Consistently, the dendritic paths and terminal segments are on average 28% and 25% shorter, respectively, in mSOD1 mice (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study's morphological analysis, as shown in Table 2.

claim: The distribution of dendritic paths is strongly skewed towards small lengths in mSOD1 immediate firing motoneurons (Kolmogorov–Smirnov bilateral test, p < 0.0001).
source: Figure 8C2 shows that the distribution of the dendritic paths is strongly skewed towards small lengths in mSOD1 mice (Kolmogorov–Smirnov bilateral test, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's morphological analysis, shown in Figure 8C2.

claim: The dendrites of immediate firing motoneurons are shorter in mSOD1 mice than in WT mice.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that the dendrites of immediate firing motoneurons are shorter in mSOD1 mice than in WT mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the morphological analysis.

claim: Only spinal motoneurons that display the immediate firing pattern undergo substantial electrical and morphological alterations in neonatal mSOD1 mice.
source: We show that only spinal motoneurons that display the immediate firing pattern undergo substantial electrical and morphological alterations in neonatal mSOD1 mice whereas no changes occur in the motoneurons displaying the delayed firing pattern.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's primary findings.

claim: No changes occur in motoneurons displaying the delayed firing pattern in neonatal mSOD1 mice.
source: We show that only spinal motoneurons that display the immediate firing pattern undergo substantial electrical and morphological alterations in neonatal mSOD1 mice whereas no changes occur in the motoneurons displaying the delayed firing pattern.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's primary findings.

claim: The dendrites of immediate firing motoneurons are about 30% shorter in mSOD1 compared to WT mice.
source: In immediate firing motoneurons, their dendrites are about 30% shorter in mSOD1 compared to WT mice.
evidence: This is a summary of the morphological findings.

claim: The immediate firing motoneurons become more excitable in mSOD1 mice.
source: Furthermore their rheobase is decreased, their voltage threshold for spiking is hyperpolarized and mixed mode oscillations are largely absent. This indicates that the immediate firing motoneurons become more excitable in mSOD1 mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological findings.

claim: The delayed firing pattern is due to the specific presence of two potassium currents: an A-current and a slowly activating and inactivating potassium current.
source: This type of firing is due to the specific presence in these motoneurons of two potassium currents that act at two time scales: an A-current and a slowly activating and inactivating potassium current (Leroy et al., SfN abstract 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the authors' previous research, supported by citation.

claim: These two potassium currents make F-type motoneurons less excitable than S-type motoneurons in neonates.
source: These two currents make the F-type motoneurons less excitable than the S-type motoneurons in neonates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the understanding of the currents' effects.

claim: The delayed firing pattern is transient and disappears with age.
source: However the delayed firing pattern is transient and disappears with age (Russier et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citation.

claim: In adults, the lower excitability of F-type motoneurons observed in WT animals is mainly due to the fact that they are much larger than S-type motoneurons.
source: In adults, the lower excitability of F-type motoneurons observed in WT animals is mainly due to the fact that they are much larger than the S-type motoneurons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about adult motoneurons.

claim: The origin of hyperexcitability in immediate firing motoneurons seems to be different from the mechanism at work in late embryonic motoneurons.
source: The origin of the hyperexcitability in the immediate firing motoneurons seems to be different from the mechanism at work in late embryonic motoneurons for which hyperexcitability arises from a decrease in input conductance (van Zundert et al., 2008; Martin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the current findings with previous research, supported by citations.

claim: Numerical simulations suggest that the decrease in input conductance in embryonic motoneurons is due to a shortening of terminal segments.
source: Numerical simulations suggest that the decrease in input conductance is due to a shortening of the terminal segments of embryonic spinal motoneurons which are much more electrotonically compact than in neonates (Martin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citation.

claim: In spinal muscular atrophy, spinal motoneurons become hyperexcitable.
source: Interestingly, in spinal muscular atrophy, another motoneuron degenerative disease, spinal motoneurons also become hyperexcitable (Mentis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citation.

claim: In spinal muscular atrophy, the increased excitability is caused both by a hyperpolarization of the spiking threshold and by a decrease in input conductance.
source: In this case, the increased excitability is caused both by an hyperpolarization of the spiking threshold and by a decrease in input conductance.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research.

claim: The shortening of the dendritic tree of immediate firing motoneurons might result from an increase in spontaneous synaptic activity occurring during embryonic life.
source: The shortening of the dendritic tree of the immediate firing motoneurons might result from an increase in spontaneous synaptic activity occurring during the embryonic life (Yvert et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis, supported by citation.

claim: Alterations in both inhibitory and excitatory synaptic inputs impinging on mSOD1 motoneurons have been reported in cultured motoneurons derived from embryos.
source: Alterations in both the inhibitory and excitatory synaptic inputs impinging on mSOD1 motoneurons, as well as the properties of their postsynaptic receptors, have been reported in cultured motoneurons derived from embryos (Carunchio et al., 2008; Chang and Martin, 2011) as well as in motoneurons from neonates (van Zundert et al., 2008) and adults (Jiang et al., 2009; Sunico et al., 2011; Wootz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citations.

claim: During a critical developmental period, the morphology of the dendritic tree deeply relies on the synaptic activity received by the dendrites.
source: It has been shown that, during a critical developmental period, the morphology of the dendritic tree deeply relies on the synaptic activity received by the dendrites (Spitzer, 2006; Cline and Haas, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citations.

claim: More synaptic inputs can lead to a shortening of dendrites.
source: More synaptic inputs can lead to a shortening of the dendrites (Tripodi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citation.

claim: Such structural homeostatic response of motoneurons might counterbalance the increase in synaptic activity to ensure that an appropriate level of input is achieved.
source: Such structural homeostatic response of the motoneurons might counterbalance the increase in synaptic activity to ensure that an appropriate level of input is achieved (Tripodi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on previous research, supported by citation.

claim: The change in voltage threshold might be a homeostatic regulation in response to synaptic hyperactivity.
source: The change in voltage threshold might also be a homeostatic regulation in response to synaptic hyperactivity.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis.

claim: The frequency of both excitatory and inhibitory spontaneous synaptic events are increased in early stages of mSOD1.
source: Since the frequency of both excitatory and synaptic spontaneous events are increased in early stages (van Zundert et al., 2008), it is possible that the net input to S-type motoneurons is shifted towards more inhibition.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citation.

claim: Synaptic hyperactivity, dendritic shrinkage and intrinsic hyperexcitability might be causally linked.
source: As suggested by van Zundert et al. (2008) synaptic hyperactivity, dendritic shrinkage and intrinsic hyperexcitability might well be causally linked.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis from previous research, supported by citation.

claim: Only S-type motoneurons display intrinsic hyperexcitability in mSOD1 neonates.
source: Our results show that only the S-type motoneurons display an intrinsic hyperexcitability in mSOD1 neonates.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's primary findings.

claim: F-type motoneurons vulnerable in ALS are not hyperexcitable.
source: On the other hand, F-type motoneurons vulnerable in ALS, are not hyperexcitable.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's primary findings.

claim: Intrinsic hyperexcitability is not an early event that triggers degeneration of motoneurons, contrary to the standard hypothesis.
source: We can therefore conclude that, contrary to the standard hypothesis (Ilieva et al., 2009), intrinsic hyperexcitabilty is not an early event that triggers degeneration of the motoneurons.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, contrasting with previous hypotheses.

claim: Degeneration of neuromuscular junctions of F-type motor units in mSOD1 mice does not start before P50.
source: In mSOD1 mice, degeneration of the neuromuscular junctions of F-type motor units does not start before P50 whereas the S-type motor units do not degenerate (Pun et al., 2006; Hegedus et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citations.

claim: S-type motor units do not degenerate in mSOD1 mice.
source: In mSOD1 mice, degeneration of the neuromuscular junctions of F-type motor units does not start before P50 whereas the S-type motor units do not degenerate (Pun et al., 2006; Hegedus et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citations.

claim: The specific dendritic shrinkage of S-type motoneurons increases the size difference between S- and F-types motoneurons.
source: The specific dendritic shrinkage of S-type motoneuron increases the size difference between S- and F- types motoneurons, and it has most likely a beneficial effect on S-type motoneurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the morphological findings.

claim: The specific dendritic shrinkage of S-type motoneurons has most likely a beneficial effect on S-type motoneurons.
source: The specific dendritic shrinkage of S-type motoneuron increases the size difference between S- and F- types motoneurons, and it has most likely a beneficial effect on S-type motoneurons.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: The smaller the total membrane surface, the smaller the metabolic demand to maintain this surface.
source: Indeed the smaller the total membrane surface, the smaller the metabolic demand to maintain this surface.
evidence: This is stated as general biological knowledge.

claim: Motoneurons cope with an energetic issue in ALS that is caused by a disruption of mitochondrial function.
source: Given the fact that motoneurons cope to an energetic issue in ALS that is caused by a disruption of the mitochondrial function (von Lewinski and Keller, 2005; Ilieva et al., 2009), a lesser energetic demand may increase their chance to survive.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citations.

claim: A lesser energetic demand may increase motoneurons' chance to survive in ALS.
source: Given the fact that motoneurons cope to an energetic issue in ALS that is caused by a disruption of the mitochondrial function (von Lewinski and Keller, 2005; Ilieva et al., 2009), a lesser energetic demand may increase their chance to survive.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on established knowledge.

claim: Specific hyperexcitability of S-type motoneurons might contribute to motoneuron survival.
source: Specific hyperexcitability of S-type motoneurons might also contribute to motoneuron survival as recently suggested (Saxena et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on recent research, supported by citation.

claim: The whole population of adult spinal motoneurons are, on average, not hyperexcitable just prior to the onset of neuromuscular junction degeneration.
source: However, the whole population of adult spinal motoneurons are, on average, not hyperexcitable just prior to the onset of neuromuscular junctions degeneration (Delestree et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research, supported by citation.

claim: Some adult motoneurons turn out to be hypoexcitable since they lose the capacity to discharge repetitively in response to stationary inputs.
source: Some of them even turn out to be hypoexcitable since they lose the capacity to discharge repetitively in response to stationary inputs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research.
